paras: The expulsion of Black waiters from Linton, Indiana, occurred on July 6, 1903, when a crowd in the mining town drove out eight Black men from Terre Haute who had come to serve an Elks banquet. The crowd threatened to dynamite the hall unless the men were sent away, and they were hurried out of town; no one was reported hurt. Coming in the week of the Evansville riot, it was cited by editors as evidence that mob action against Black people was spreading in the North.

Linton was described as a town where no Black person was allowed to live, a policy the Associated Press traced to 1896. That year, the wire said, a coal company brought in 300 Black men to replace strikers; after one was said to have shot a white boy, whites drove all of them out, several being shot.
On July 6 an Elks lodge was instituted at Linton, and its hosts engaged a Terre Haute caterer, named in the wire as Alex Sanderson and later as Alec Sandison, who brought his cook and waiters.

According to the Indianapolis Journal's Linton correspondent, the men's arrival prompted street-corner talk, and by nightfall about 2,000 people filled the streets. "Self-delegated leaders" addressed the crowd, a vote was taken, and a committee was appointed to have the caterer send the men away, under the slogan "Peace if possible, but force if necessary." The Associated Press reported that miners gathered outside during the lodge ceremony and threatened to dynamite the hall unless the Black men were sent out of town.

The wire said the eight men were hurried into a cab and driven to Jasonville, where they took a train for Terre Haute, while six policemen hung on the carriage and beat back the crowd. The Journal's correspondent instead described a covered wagon driven toward Vigo County as the crowd cheered; the Elks' program then went on. He added that many in the crowd disapproved of the "deportation" but would do nothing to stop it.

No report of arrests was found; a New Hampshire editorial noted that no one in that summer's outbreaks had been punished. On July 11 the labor leader Eugene V. Debs called the expulsion the work of a mob of union miners and said the union, then appealing to Black miners in Kentucky and West Virginia, should disavow it. He called it "an utter repudiation of the union's professions." The Journal also reported a claim that the Elks' blackballing of many Linton men was one cause of the demonstration.

Before a circus with Black employees played Linton on July 13, Governor Durbin telephoned Sandison and the sheriff and suggested swearing in deputies; the show left its Black workers behind. On July 17 a Linton "committee" letter told Charles Shelton, a Black resident of Bloomfield, that the town's Black residents must leave Greene County by July 25, a threat the Courier-Journal linked to "the recent riot at Linton."

The wire story ran on July 7 and 8 from Richmond and Birmingham to St. Louis, Salt Lake City and Rock Island. Its headlines ranged from "NEGROES DRIVEN FROM LINTON" and "TRIED TO KILL NEGROES" to the Birmingham Age-Herald's "NEGROES CAUSE ANOTHER RIOT," whose subhead nonetheless described policemen beating back "the pursuing mob of whites." Indiana's Plymouth Tribune used a racial slur in a subhead.

The Indianapolis Journal called it a "race hatred epidemic" and said the men were driven out "simply because they were colored," though its headline stressed that no violence was offered. Editorials in Alexandria, San Antonio and Manchester, New Hampshire, condemned the summer's attacks, the San Antonio Daily Light saying the victims' "only offence" was "the color of their skins." Southern papers turned the story against the North: the Savannah Morning News needled the Indianapolis News, and a Kentucky weekly said such total exclusion existed "nowhere in the South." No Black-press account of the episode was found.

The wire gave the crowd as several hundred or several thousand miners; the Journal and two Terre Haute specials said 2,000. The Journal described a peaceful removal at nightfall; wire copies had the men arriving in the afternoon and narrowly escaping death.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal Linton correspondent
accounts.gist: A crowd of 2,000 gathered by nightfall, voted, sent a committee to the caterer and cheered as the waiters were driven off in a covered wagon toward Vigo County; there was 'no serious rioting or violence'.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Several hundred (in other copies several thousand) miners threatened to dynamite the hall; the eight men, who 'narrowly escaped' with their lives, were hurried by cab to Jasonville under a guard of six policemen and put on a train for Terre Haute.

accounts.label: Terre Haute specials
accounts.gist: Sandison was ordered to send the men out of Linton, and a mob of 2,000 expedited their departure; one report said Linton men's rejection by the Elks was a cause.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal called it a 'race hatred epidemic' and said the men were driven out 'simply because they were colored', while heading the story 'NO VIOLENCE WAS OFFERED'.
AP copies ran under headlines from 'NEGROES DRIVEN FROM LINTON' and 'TRIED TO KILL NEGROES' to the Age-Herald's 'NEGROES CAUSE ANOTHER RIOT'; the Plymouth Tribune used a slur in a subhead.
Editorials in Alexandria, San Antonio and Manchester, N.H., treated Linton as part of a spreading mob law against Black people, the last comparing it to Russia's persecution of Jews.
Southern and border papers used Linton to rebuke the North: the Savannah Morning News jabbed at the Indianapolis News and the Bourbon News said such exclusion existed nowhere in the South.
The Democratic Advocate's 'The North Takes Up Lynching' listed Linton among Northern outbreaks in an editorial that defended Southern disfranchisement.

conflicts.note: The AP text varies between copies (several hundred in A8 and A6; several thousand in A9, A4, A10 and A11); the Indianapolis Journal's correspondent and two Terre Haute specials give 2,000 and describe townspeople generally, not only miners.

record_check.dossier: Eight unnamed Black men from Terre Haute, cook(s) and waiters of caterer Alex Sanderson (Sandison); one editorial says a cook and eight waiters.
A crowd of Linton miners and townspeople; Debs called it a mob of union miners. No individual named.

No crime alleged; the men were Black in a town where 'no negro is allowed', a policy traced to the 1896 ouster of Black strikebreakers. One report also cited Linton men's being blackballed by the Elks.

Conflicts on crowd size, conveyance, whether violence occurred, and time of day.
